title: De eximio usu methodi interpolationum in serierum doctrina

deep.reconstruction:
Context: E555 uses an interpolation method to expand an arc Phi in a series of sines sin(a Phi), sin(b Phi), ... with frequencies a = m, b = 1-m, c = 1+m, ... The previous page specializes to n = 1-m. Comparing the resulting coefficients with Beta integrals, Euler gets a constant M defined by integrals, the expansion M Phi = sum_j sin((m+j)Phi)/(m+j)^2, and by differentiation M = sum_j cos((m+j)Phi)/(m+j). Setting Phi = 0 gives M = 1/m + sum_k 2m/(m^2-k^2) = pi cot(m pi). Equating the two expressions for M gives a relation among Beta integrals.

This page (pp. 180-181):
(i) Euler rewrites that relation, using integrals from 0 to 1. The first form is int x^m(1-x)^{m-1} dx = (1-m) pi cot(m pi) * int x^m(1-x)^{-2m} dx / int x^m(1-x)^{-m} dx, i.e. B(m+1,m) = (1-m) pi cot(m pi) B(m+1,1-2m)/B(m+1,1-m). The 'more elegant' form is B(m,m) = 2 pi cot(m pi) B(m,1-2m)/B(m,1-m).

(ii) Corollary 1 (sec. 26). Grouping the terms as sum over j in Z of cos((m+j)phi)/(m+j) = pi cot(m pi), for every angle phi.
- Using cos((k +/- m)phi) = cos k phi cos m phi -/+ sin k phi sin m phi, he gets pi cot(m pi) = cos(m phi)[1/m - 2m sum_k cos(k phi)/(k^2-m^2)] - 2 sin(m phi) sum_k k sin(k phi)/(k^2-m^2).
- With m phi = pi/2 this gives a sum of k sin(k pi/(2m))/(k^2-m^2).

(iii) Corollary 2 (sec. 27). Integrating Corollary 1 in phi gives pi phi cot(m pi) = sum_j sin((m+j)phi)/(m+j)^2. Two special cases:
- phi = pi gives pi^2 cos(m pi)/sin^2(m pi) = 1/m^2 - 1/(1-m)^2 - 1/(1+m)^2 + 1/(2-m)^2 + 1/(2+m)^2 - ..., i.e. sum_j (-1)^j/(m+j)^2.
- m phi = pi gives pi^2 cot(m pi)/(4m^2) = sum_k k sin(k pi/m)/(k^2-m^2)^2.

(iv) Corollary 3 (sec. 28). B(m,m) B(m,1-m) = 2 pi cot(m pi) B(m,1-2m). With m = lambda/n and x = y^n this becomes Euler's (p/q) integrals int y^{lambda-1}(1-y^n)^{(q-n)/n} dy.

(v) Scholion (sec. 29, continued on the next page). Euler says a direct proof seems arduous, but it follows from his earlier results on these integrals: (lambda/(n-lambda)) = pi/(n sin(lambda pi/n)) and the three-term sine relation. In modern terms this is B(m,m)/B(m,1-2m) = sin(2m pi)/sin(m pi) = 2 cos(m pi), which follows from Gamma reflection.

Purpose: harvesting identities (Beta-integral relations and trigonometric series) from the sine-interpolation/expansion of the arc.
errors: 'Si phi denotet angulum quemcunque' is too strong. The sum over j of cos((m+j)phi)/(m+j) equals pi cot(m pi) only for |phi| < 2 pi. Indeed sum_j e^{i(m+j)phi}/(m+j) = pi e^{i pi m}/sin(pi m) for 0 < phi < 2 pi. For 2 pi < phi < 4 pi the sum is pi cos(3m pi)/sin(m pi) instead. Likewise pi phi cot(m pi) = sum_j sin((m+j)phi)/(m+j)^2 holds only for |phi| <= 2 pi. Consequently the case phi = pi/(2m) needs m > 1/4, and phi = pi/m needs m >= 1/2.
In the special case m phi = pi/2 the printed equation omits a factor: correctly -1/2 pi cot(m pi) = sum_k k sin(k pi/(2m))/(k^2-m^2), not pi cot(m pi) = sum ... as printed.
The second bracket of the decomposed form in Corollary 1 ends with '- etc.'; all terms are positive, so it should read '+ etc.'.
None in the Beta identities: B(m+1,m) = cos(m pi) B(m,1-2m) and B(m,m) B(m,1-m) = 2 pi cot(m pi) B(m,1-2m) both check via Gamma reflection.

ideas.what: Beta-integral identity B(m,m) B(m,1-m) = 2 pi cot(m pi) B(m,1-2m), equivalently B(m,m) = 2 cos(m pi) B(m,1-2m), and the version with x = y^n
ideas.modern_name: Consequence of Euler's reflection formula Gamma(m)Gamma(1-m) = pi/sin(m pi)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (reflection formula, and the (p/q) integral calculus of the 1760s-70s)
ideas.where_published: Euler's papers on integrals int x^{p-1}(1-x^n)^{q/n-1} dx (Observationes circa integralia formularum..., E321, and related papers); the Scholion itself cites them

ideas.where_published: Similar series appear in Euler's later trigonometric-series papers; exact precedence unsure

missed.claim: Euler's interpolation method expands phi in sines with the shifted-integer frequencies {m+j : j in Z}. This is an early instance of an explicit non-harmonic Fourier expansion. The coefficients are computed from infinite interpolation products, Lagrange-style, which ties them to the later theory of non-harmonic Fourier series. That theory (Paley-Wiener, Levinson, Kadec 1/4 theorem) treats {e^{i(j+m)x}} as a Riesz basis, with coefficient formulas given by infinite products of sine-type entire functions. Histories of non-harmonic Fourier series do not usually cite E555.
missed.quote: pi phi cos. m pi / sin. m pi = sin. m phi/mm - sin.(1-m)phi/(1-m)^2 + sin.(1+m)phi/(1+m)^2 - ...
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Historical precedence for biorthogonal expansions via interpolation products. Euler's validity claim ('any angle') also misses the interval restriction |phi| <= 2 pi, which is exactly where completeness/representability matters.

deep.surprise_reason: The identities are correct consequences of Gamma reflection and standard Fourier series, apart from an overly broad validity claim and a dropped factor. The only mildly notable aspect is that they come from an interpolation-based non-harmonic sine expansion, which is rarely linked historically to Paley-Wiener theory.
transcription_corrections: First display: the exponent of x is m, not n: int x^m dx(1-x)^{m-1} = (1-m) pi cos m pi/sin m pi * int x^m dx(1-x)^{-2m} / int x^m dx(1-x)^{-m}.
Second display: int x^{m-1}dx(1-x)^{m-1} = 2 pi cos m pi/sin m pi * int x^{m-1}dx(1-x)^{-2m} / int x^{m-1}dx(1-x)^{-m} (m-1, not n-1). The x = y^n substitution in sec. 28 confirms this.
Sec. 28: all three integrals have x^{m-1}, not x^{n-1}.
Corollary 1, second bracket: final '- etc.' should be '+ etc.'.
Page numbers of the next page are 182/183, not 162/163.
